name: Social Determinants of Health
title: Social Determinants of Health
answer: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping daily life. In epidemiology and population health, they include income, education, housing, food access, transportation, social support, and exposure to discrimination. AI models in this area use these variables to predict individual and community health risks, identify unmet needs, and target interventions. The scope extends from descriptive analysis of neighborhood deprivation to causal inference about how policy changes affect health outcomes.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping daily life. In epidemiology and population health, they include income, education, housing, food access, transportation, social support, and exposure to discrimination. AI models in this area use these variables to predict individual and community health risks, identify unmet needs, and target interventions. The scope extends from descriptive analysis of neighborhood deprivation to causal inference about how policy changes affect health outcomes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: SDOH models run on linked data infrastructure that combines clinical records, insurance claims, public health surveillance, census data, and community-level indicators such as housing quality or food desert maps. These datasets are often stored in cloud data warehouses or secure research environments, with geocoding to attach neighborhood characteristics to patient addresses. Compute needs are modest compared to imaging or genomic models, but data integration and identity resolution across sources are the main engineering challenges. Some deployments run inside health system firewalls, while population-level dashboards may use public cloud services.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work typically begins with feature engineering from structured fields such as zip code, insurance type, and ICD-10 Z codes that capture housing or food insecurity. Analysts then fit models ranging from logistic regression and survival analysis to gradient-boosted trees and, less often, deep learning on free-text notes. Model outputs are usually risk scores or predicted probabilities of hospitalization, readmission, or chronic disease onset, adjusted for clinical comorbidities. Causal methods such as propensity score matching or difference-in-differences are used when the goal is to estimate the effect of a social program rather than to predict an outcome.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: SDOH models raise distinct governance concerns because they encode sensitive information about poverty, race, immigration status, and neighborhood conditions, often inferred from proxies rather than directly measured. Risk of algorithmic discrimination is high when models use zip code or credit data as stand-ins for protected characteristics, and when predictions influence care management or resource allocation. Data provenance is often unclear because social variables come from third-party vendors or outdated census tracts, and patients rarely know these data are being used. Oversight typically involves institutional review boards, health system data governance committees, and, where models affect coverage or benefits, state and federal nondiscrimination rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward models that not only predict risk but also recommend specific social interventions, such as food delivery, housing support, or transportation vouchers, and then measure their effect on health outcomes. Real-time linkage to benefit enrollment systems, wearable devices, and community health worker records is likely to replace static annual census data. There is growing interest in causal machine learning and federated learning across health systems to estimate treatment effects without pooling sensitive patient data. At the same time, patient and community oversight is becoming a standard part of model development, and regulators are beginning to ask for evidence that SDOH models reduce disparities rather than widen them.
